title: Lamb Nihari
subtitle: A slow-braised Mughal lamb stew with warm spices and a silky gravy
excerpt: Lamb shoulder cooked for hours in a spiced gravy until the meat is falling-tender. A Friday-morning dish from the streets of Delhi and Karachi, best eaten with naan.
sourceNotes: Nihari originated in the royal kitchens of Mughal Delhi; this version draws on Pakistani and North Indian home-cooking traditions using lamb shoulder.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to three months. The spice deepens after freezing. Defrost overnight and reheat gently, adding a splash of water.
recipe.batchNotes: Nihari is ideal for batch cooking. Double the recipe in a large pot and the cooking time stays the same.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Traditionally made overnight and eaten at breakfast. Cook the day before for the best flavour.

content.text: Nihari is a patience dish. The lamb needs three hours at the lowest possible heat to break down properly. The gravy is thickened with flour, not reduced by boiling, which gives it a distinctive, almost silky texture.

items.prepNote: bone-in, cut into large pieces by the butcher
cut into fine matchsticks, to serve

content.text: Heat two tablespoons of ghee in the Dutch oven over a high heat. Fry the onions, stirring, for 12 to 15 minutes until deep golden brown. Remove with a slotted spoon and set aside.
Add the remaining ghee to the pot. Brown the lamb pieces in batches over a high heat, two minutes per side. Transfer to a plate.
Lower the heat to medium. Add the garlic and ginger paste and stir for two minutes. Add all the ground spices and salt. Stir for one minute.
Stir the flour into the spice paste and cook for two minutes. Gradually add the stock, stirring all the time to prevent lumps.
Return the lamb and fried onions to the pot. The liquid should come just over halfway up the meat. Bring to the edge of a simmer.
Cover tightly and cook on the lowest possible heat for two and a half to three hours. The lamb should be very tender and starting to come away from the bone.
Taste the gravy and adjust salt. Serve in deep bowls, topped with ginger matchsticks, fresh coriander, green chilli and a squeeze of lemon.

items.cause: The flour was added too quickly, or the stock was too cold.
items.fix: Add the stock a ladleful at a time, stirring constantly. If lumps form, pass the gravy through a sieve before adding the lamb back.

items.symptom: The lamb is still tough after three hours.
items.cause: The heat was too low or the pot lost its seal.
items.fix: Check the lid is sealed tightly. Give the lamb another 30 minutes. Shoulder pieces vary in size, so some need longer.

items.cause: The pot was not sealed tightly enough and steam escaped.
items.fix: Remove the lid and boil briskly for 10 minutes to reduce. Stir often so the base does not catch.
